BOARD OF SCHOOL COMMITTEE 
MANCHESTER SCHOOL DISTRICT SAU #37 
 
Monday, August 10, 2026 6:30 p.m.  
 
1. Mayor Ruais called the meeting to order at 6:30 p.m. 
 
2. Mayor Ruais called for the Pledge of Allegiance and asked Committee Member Taylor to lead 
us in the Pledge. 
 
3. A moment of silence was observed.  
 
Vice Chairman O'Connell asked the Board and the community to keep the family of Sandy Wenzel in 
their thoughts and prayers. He noted that Ms. Wenzell had been a longtime crossing guard at 
Bakersville and was loved by the community. 
 
4. The Clerk called the roll.  
 
Present:  Committee Members Turner, Georges, Want, Taylor, Bergeron, Stewart, 
O’Connell, Potter, St. John, Garrity, Hamer, O’Neil-Wong, Smith and 
Mayor Ruais. 
 
Absent: Committee Members Parr and Bergeron. 
 
 
5.        RECOGNITIONS 
 
There were no recognitions this evening. 
 
6. PUBLIC FORUM 
 
The purpose of the public forum is to give the residents of Manchester the opportunity to 
address the board.  All people wishing to speak will have up to three (3) minutes to do so, and 
any comments must be directed to the chair.  Any resident wishing to speak will come forward 
to the nearest microphone, clearly state their name and address when recognized and give their 
comments.  
 
Speakers may offer comments on school operations and programs that concern them.  In public 
session, however, the Board shall not hear personal complaints of school personnel or 
complaints against any person connected with the District.  Other channels are provided for 
Board consideration and disposition of legitimate complaints involving  school district 
employees, which should be referred to the Superintendent.  Speakers are requested to refrain

from providing confidential information during this comment period.  Any comments that are 
given regarding personnel matters will not be responded to by the Board or Administration 
during the public meeting, as these items should be discussed in non-public session.   
 
 
Amy Kereage, Executive Director of Manchester Proud: 
She thanked the Mayor and members of the Board of School Committee and provided an update 
regarding Celebrate Ed 2026: Welcome Back Manchester.  She stated that the event would be held on 
August 20 from 4:00 to 7:00 p.m. at Victory Park and the Welcome Center. She explained that Celebrate 
Ed is one of Manchester Proud's signature events and was entering its sixth year. She thanked Committee 
Member Stewart for participating on the planning team. Ms. Kereage explained that the previous year 
Manchester Proud had reimagined Celebrate Ed with a greater focus on celebrating the return to school 
and making sure Manchester students and families had the resources they needed to begin the school 
year strong. She stated that the event had continued to grow and that Manchester Proud believed it was 
now the largest back-to-school celebration in New Hampshire. Ms. Kereage said that at its heart, 
Celebrate Ed was about reducing barriers, supporting families, and creating a positive and exciting start 
to the school year. She cited Manchester Proud's partnership with Gear Up for Schools as an example. 
She reported that the organization had prepared 3,275 backpacks just the previous week for New 
Hampshire students in schools, foster care, military families, and communities served through partner 
organizations. Of those backpacks, 1,000 were scheduled to be distributed at Celebrate Ed, with 
sponsorship support from Costco and Catholic Medical Center. Ms. Kereage reported that families would 
also have access to clothing provided by Brookside Thrift Store and Apparel Impact. The Lions Club 
would sponsor the bookmobile and would also provide vision screenings during the event. 
Approximately 25 hair professionals were expected to participate and provide haircuts, barbering, and 
braiding services. Free food and other resources would also be available to families. Ms. Kereage stated 
that what excited her most was the collaboration that made the event possible. She reported that 87 
community partners were scheduled to table at the event, the largest number to date. She stated that: 
 MTA would provide free transportation downtown for families; 
 The Health Department would provide a van for Lions Club vision screenings; 
 Manchester Police and Fire would participate with their vehicles; 
 The Manchester School District would be at the Welcome Center assisting families with school 
registration; and 
 Numerous organizations would provide school supplies, clothing, food, books, health services, 
and additional family resources.
August 10, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 3 of 36 
 
Ms. Kereage emphasized that a backpack, new clothing, a haircut, a book, a vision screening, 
transportation, or help with school registration could make a real difference for a family preparing for a 
new school year. She stated that bringing all of those resources together in one welcoming location 
helped reduce barriers while showing families how many people and organizations throughout 
Manchester were invested in their success.  Ms. Kereage stated that this community collaboration was 
what made Celebrate Ed so special. She invited Board members to attend again and encouraged them to 
share information about the event with their constituents. 
 
Matt Courchesne, 167 Sagmore Street: 
Mr. Courchesne stated that since 2007 he had worked with some of Manchester's most at-risk children 
through Helping Our Pupils Excel New Hampshire, Inc., the nonprofit organization he founded in 2012, 
and before that through the YMCA STAY program. He stated that his responsibility was to the families 
and children his organization served and that he answered to them. Mr. Courchesne stated that over the 
previous 19 years he had watched children overcome trauma related to adverse childhood experiences 
and what at times seemed like impossible odds. He said he knew what successful schools looked like 
because he had been part of the process of changing children's lives in the school setting and stated that 
Bakersville Elementary had been one of those schools. Mr. Courchesne stated that he had not addressed 
the Board in almost seven years, but that the changes he had witnessed at Bakersville since 
implementation of the Dual Language Immersion program compelled him to speak. Before coming to 
the meeting, Mr. Courchesne said he had reached out privately to three Board members. He said that one 
Board member specifically told him that he did not understand the program and was spreading 
misinformation.  Mr. Courchesne stated that what he did understand was that he had been part of the 
Bakersville building for the previous five years, investing both time and money. He stated that he had 
worked with the entire school, had seen the implementation of DLI, and had witnessed what he believed 
was a change in culture within the Bakersville community. He characterized his experience as firsthand 
rather than theoretical. Mr. Courchesne questioned how many of the Board members who had 
participated in the previous term's 14-0 vote had asked a teacher whether DLI was the right fit for 
Bakersville. He stated that what he had seen presented publicly was a local article that, in his opinion, 
read more like a public relations piece than a true evaluation. He stated that in one of his conversations, 
that article had been cited as evidence that the program was succeeding. Mr. Courchesne said that 
throughout his experience working with publicly funded programs, decisions were supposed to be driven 
by evidence rather than promotional stories. He stated that the evidence he saw was what he characterized
August 10, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 4 of 36 
 
as an exodus of teachers leaving Bakersville. Mr. Courchesne stated that all four Dual Language 
Immersion teachers from the previous year had left their positions and that after approximately a decade 
at Bakersville, the school's principal had also left. He stated that when an entire instructional team turned 
over during implementation of a major initiative, that should prompt questions rather than assumptions 
that everything was going well. Mr. Courchesne also expressed concern regarding the effect the program 
could have on Bakersville as a neighborhood school. He stated that as the program expanded, families 
could have fewer meaningful choices if they discovered DLI was not the right fit for their child. He 
stated that parents should not have to choose between remaining in a specialized program and remaining 
in their neighborhood school. Mr. Courchesne concluded by requesting one specific action from the 
Board: that it review the implementation and outcomes of the Dual Language Immersion program at 
Bakersville. He stated that Bakersville had been known for strong leadership, dedicated teachers, and 
meaningful community partnerships, and that if there were warning signs that those strengths were 
changing, the Board had a responsibility to examine those changes. 
 
Jason Bonilla , of 463 Central Street: 
Mr. Bonilla first addressed the previous comments regarding Dual Language Immersion. He stated that 
he and Mr. Courchesne had previously discussed the issue and emphasized that families had been 
consulted regarding the program. Mr. Bonilla stated that he had personally been present for those 
conversations and remembered families crying because they felt they were finally going to have an 
opportunity to be part of their children's education. He stated that the District had spoken with numerous 
families and that DLI was not something that had simply been created without input. Mr. Bonilla also 
stated that he was himself a product of dual language immersion.  He then shifted to the NG, or No 
Grade, policy, stating that he had heard considerable discussion in the background about potentially 
bringing the policy back. Mr. Bonilla acknowledged that overall absenteeism continued to be a 
significant challenge. He stated, however, that the first question the District needed to ask was, why were 
students not coming to school? He asked whether attendance problems involved a specific demographic 
of students. He questioned whether the students involved were high-honors or Advanced Placement 
students. He asked whether students were not coming to school because of: 
 Bullying; 
 Bussing or transportation difficulties; 
 A lack of classroom engagement; or 
 Other barriers affecting students and families.
August 10, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 5 of 36 
 
 
Mr. Bonilla questioned whether the District had individuals checking in with families in person, rather 
than communicating only through telephone calls or email. He also asked whether the District was 
leaning sufficiently on community partners to support efforts to get children to school, outside of work 
the City was already doing through initiatives such as the walking bus. Mr. Bonilla stated that when he 
had served on the Board of School Committee, the Board had removed the NG policy knowing that 
doing so was a first step toward finding a better way to get children to school rather than simply resorting 
to what he characterized as the easiest response of altering their GPA. He said he frequently heard the 
phrase "preparing students for real life" and had heard that term throughout his four years on the Board. 
However, he stated that identifying the true barriers preventing students from attending school was also 
part of real life. Mr. Bonilla concluded that the District should first determine why students were not 
coming to school and then navigate the challenge of helping them attend school consistently and arrive 
on time.

7. Response to Public Comment 
 (Note:  Motions limited to sending items to Committees only.) 
 
Superintendent Chmiel stated that she wanted to take time and consideration in responding to the 
comments made regarding the District's Dual Language Immersion programming.  She strongly 
disagreed with the suggestion that the former Bakersville principal had left because of DLI and 
indicated that she had communicated with the former principal to make sure she was not missing 
information.  Superintendent Chmiel stated that associating the principal's departure with DLI was 
inappropriate.  She likewise objected to attributing staff departures to the DLI program, emphasizing
August 10, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 6 of 36 
 
that members of the public did not have a right to know the personal circumstances affecting individual 
employees' decisions. She also disagreed with the assertions that DLI was hurting children or that the 
District had failed to consider data or the impact of the program on the Bakersville community. 
She noted that Ms. Perron and Bakersville's new principal were present and could answer specific 
questions regarding the program.  Superintendent Chmiel stated that she was extremely concerned by 
the characterization of the DLI program presented during public comment. 
 
Committee Member Stewart also responded to Mr. Courchesne's comments. She stated that she was 
one of the School Board members who had held several conversations with him. She said that Mr. 
Courchesne had repeatedly asked questions and that she had provided him with data supporting the 
DLI program. Committee Member Stewart disagreed with the suggestion that District programming 
decisions were not being made based upon evidence and facts, particularly when Mr. Courchesne was 
relying on what she viewed as his own anecdotal experience as evidence.  She stated that she felt 
strongly about DLI and was proud of the work staff had invested in the program. She stated that 
students were excelling and that she believed the program was thriving. She concluded by respectfully 
asking Mr. Courchesne to stop spreading what she considered misinformation regarding DLI. 
 
Superintendent Chmiel asked for confirmation that DLI would be addressed through the Teaching and 
Learning Committee.  The Administration confirmed that a brief update would be provided and that a 
more comprehensive DLI presentation, including data, would be presented in September.  
Superintendent Chmiel noted that DLI had already been presented to Teaching and Learning multiple 
times during the time the program had been operating in the District. Administration confirmed that 
DLI updates were generally brought to the committee at least three times per year to keep the Board 
informed.  Dr. Chmiel reminded the public that agendas and meeting notes containing DLI information 
were posted online and available for public review. 
 
Vice Chairman O'Connell stated that his interest was in seeing the data. He said the data would ultimately 
show whether the program was thriving and successful or whether it was not.  He noted that individuals 
who questioned the program should be able to review the same evidence being provided to the Board. 
Administration confirmed that the data would be presented at the September Teaching and Learning 
Committee meeting.

Ms. Perron provided several preliminary data points regarding implementation and outcomes.  She 
noted that a full update had previously been provided to the State Board of Education in early June. 
She reported that: 
 72% of Bakersville first graders grew one or more reading levels as measured by the Spanish 
literacy assessment; 
 58% of kindergarten students grew one or more reading levels; 
 100% of rising first graders had elected to remain in the program; 
 All but one rising second grader were remaining in the program, with the one student leaving 
because the family was moving out of state; and 
 15 students participated in a Spanish-English Dual Language summer program. 
 
Ms. Perron stated that these data points indicated positive student outcomes and strong parent 
engagement. She acknowledged that a new program naturally experiences growing pains and 
challenges and stated that some staffing challenges had been anticipated. She also noted that some 
employee departures were connected to individual personnel decisions that could not appropriately be 
discussed publicly. Ms. Perron stated that the available indicators suggested strong community support 
for the program and reiterated that a full presentation would be provided to Teaching and Learning in 
September. 
 
Bakersville's principal, Bryan Watson, echoed Superintendent Chmiel's comments regarding employee 
departures. He stated that there were many reasons teachers might leave and that it was not appropriate 
for Mr. Courchesne to tell the Board why individual teachers had left without knowing their personal 
circumstances. He acknowledged that Mr. Courchesne had been a significant asset to Bakersville and 
had helped the school in many ways. However, he stated that Mr. Courchesne did not speak for 
Bakersville or its teachers regarding the DLI program.  He stated that the program was successful 
while acknowledging that it had challenges because it was new. Although new to the principal 
position, he noted that he had served as assistant principal at Bakersville for seven years. He stated that 
the culture at Bakersville was strong, the program was strong, and the school would continue moving 
forward and improving the program.
August 10, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 8 of 36 
 
It was asked what role Mr. Courchesne had held at Bakersville.  Principal Watson explained that Mr. 
Courchesne had participated through HOPE New Hampshire, a nonprofit organization, and had 
provided support that included: 
 Pizza parties for attendance winners; 
 Staff outings; 
 Field trips; 
 Monetary support for students; and 
 Involvement with the Elmwood community and students connected with the Elmwood projects. 
 
He also addressed overflow enrollment, stating that the prior year Bakersville had approximately 13 
students from other schools attending the school and approximately six overflow students related to 
DLI. A Board member stated that she had visited the DLI  program at Weston and had been impressed 
watching students participating in French instruction.  She said students appeared highly engaged and 
expressed excitement regarding DLI.   
 
Ms. Perron emphasized that Bakersville's DLI participation reflected service to the neighborhood 
community. She stated that students from the Bakersville community were choosing DLI and noted 
that students in two of the three classrooms were selecting the program. 
 
Committee Member Hamer thanked Mr. Bonilla for raising the attendance issue.  As Chair of the 
Student Conduct Committee, Committee Member Hamer stated that during the previous several 
months he had heard from numerous individuals, including faculty members and parents, regarding 
attendance concerns.  He acknowledged that the District had made progress over the previous several 
years but stated that significant questions remained regarding why students were not coming to school. 
He said another issue being raised was students cutting individual classes.  Committee Member Hamer 
reported that he had met with Dr. Espinola several times over the summer to discuss gathering 
attendance data.  He stated that the Student Conduct Committee hoped to begin reviewing that 
information and discussing the issue at its meeting the following week.  He recognized that additional 
data would likely be necessary but said the initial information would provide a starting point. 
 
Committee Member Hamer stated that one of his goals for the committee over the coming year was to 
dig into the attendance data, identify the causes of the problem, and determine what the District could
August 10, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 9 of 36 
 
implement to address it.  He acknowledged that this work could ultimately lead to policy changes that 
would need to move through the Policy Committee and then to the full Board for approval. 
He assured the public that the committee would continue moving forward and would make attendance a 
significant priority during the upcoming year. 
 
Attendance is not a problem exclusive to Manchester or New Hampshire.  Conversations with 
individuals in New York, Indiana, Pennsylvania, and Massachusetts demonstrated that student 
attendance was a nationwide issue, not one occurring solely within Manchester or surrounding New 
Hampshire districts. 
 
Committee Member Want asked which committee would address the NG, or No Grade, issue. 
Superintendent Chmiel stated that NG would move through Teaching and Learning and/or Policy, 
while attendance issues would move through the Student Conduct Committee. She stated that the work 
of multiple committees would likely need to be synthesized so everyone was communicating and any 
policy changes and implementation plans were properly coordinated. 
 
Many questions needed to be answered before the District considered reinstating previous practices. 
The member recalled that when the prior change had been made, the Board had expected to receive 
data the following year and expressed uncertainty as to whether all of the data had been aggregated as 
originally anticipated.  Comprehensive information is necessary so the Board could make an informed 
decision.  The Administration also reminded the Board that the District must account for the new Ed 
306 competency requirements and ensure that students were not improperly penalized for attendance 
when grading was intended to measure what students know and are able to demonstrate.

11. Superintendent’s Communications.  
 
a) Superintendent Updates: 
 
Superintendent Chmiel welcomed the Board and community back for the new school year. 
She explained that the information being presented was current as of the day of the meeting. Because 
the numbers were changing rapidly, administration had not prepared a handout in advance but would 
make the information available following the meeting. 
 
1. In-District Transfer Requests 
 
Superintendent Chmiel reported that in-district transfer requests had continued coming into the District 
following changes at the state level. In accordance with District policy, administration had been 
attempting to hold two seats at each school whenever possible. She emphasized that this could only be 
done when space was actually available. If a school was already at capacity, seats could not be held. 
The purpose of holding seats was to provide room for families who moved within Manchester near the 
end of the summer or beginning of the school year.  As of August 10, administration had received 177 
transfer requests, with 108 approved. 
 
The Superintendent provided the following approximate breakdown:  Elementary schools: 86 requests; 
approximately 40 approved; Middle schools: 37 requests; all 37 approved; High schools: 64 requests; 
51 approved. 
 
She reported significant interest in transfers to Southside and Memorial. Administration would 
continue reviewing transfer requests as they were received and would update the Board at its next 
meeting.
August 10, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 12 of 36 
 
 
2. Elementary Enrollment and Class Capacity 
 
Superintendent Chmiel stated that registration continued to progress well and that administration was 
closely monitoring elementary enrollment and class size.  Several schools and grade levels had reached 
capacity, including: 
Kindergarten - Green Acres 
Grade 1 – McDonough, Northwest, Parker-Varney, Smyth, Weston 
Grade 2 - Green Acres, Highland-Goffe's Falls, McDonough, Webster, Weston 
Grade 3 -  Green Acres, Highland-Goffe's Falls, Jewett, Weston 
Grade 4 - Green Acres, Jewett, McDonough 
 
Dr. Chmiel explained that the District was not accepting additional transfer requests into those grade 
levels at those schools at that time. She emphasized that late summer is traditionally a period of 
considerable enrollment movement as families finalize plans, move into Manchester, move within the 
City, or leave the District. The Administration would continue working closely with principals, 
monitor enrollment, make adjustments as necessary, and attempt to maintain class sizes within District 
guidelines. She stated that more comprehensive enrollment updates would be provided as registration 
stabilized closer to the opening of school. 
 
Questions and comments from the Board included: 
1. It is positive that the District had been able to accommodate many transfer requests but 
cautioned that the process should be balanced against the possibility of creating unwanted 
secondary transfers or displacing students. 
2. It was suggested that if holding two seats proved insufficient, administration should consider 
increasing the number.  Superintendent Chmiel responded that this was the first year the 
District had operated under the process in this manner and that the volume of requests was 
higher than administration had expected.  She said the District had attempted to be as 
accommodating as possible while also reserving seats.  As the start of school approached, 
administration would review final enrollment and make adjustments.  It was noted that the 
policy provided administration with latitude to determine how many seats should be reserved.
August 10, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 13 of 36 
 
If two seats proved insufficient, the District could revise its practice and report the change to 
the Board. 
3. Vice Chairman O'Connell requested that future information include a snapshot of students who 
were already attending schools outside their neighborhood assignment because of previous 
overflow situations.  He noted that once a child had established relationships and friendships at 
a school, families often would not want to move the child back even if capacity later became 
available at the neighborhood school. Siblings could also affect those decisions.  He suggested 
that understanding the number of students already outside their neighborhood schools would 
provide useful context when evaluating the new transfer policy.  The Administration explained 
that each spring principals contact families whose children had previously been placed outside 
their neighborhood school because of overflow.  If the neighborhood school has space, families 
are given the option either to return or to remain in the school where the child has already built 
relationships and friendships. 
4. Vice Chairman O'Connell encouraged the District to use the current year as a starting point for 
longitudinal data collection. He stated that the District had sometimes struggled historically to 
look back and identify patterns because information was gathered for one year but not 
necessarily maintained in a manner that allowed easy comparison. He suggested tracking 
transfers over multiple years so future Boards could determine whether transfer activity was 
increasing, decreasing, or changing in other meaningful ways. 
5. Superintendent Chmiel stated that some out-of-district transfer matters would be addressed in 
non-public session.  She reported that those requests had begun to increase somewhat during 
the previous week and stated that administration expected to have better numbers closer to 
August 24. 
6. It was referenced about the strong interest observed during the MST High School open house 
the previous spring and asked how many students had applied, how many had been admitted, 
whether the class was full, and whether any applicants had been denied.  The Administration 
responded that all students who applied by the June 30 deadline had been admitted. 
7. Concern was expressed about the effect of transfers at the high school level on classes that 
already operated with relatively low enrollment.  It was noted that certain courses were 
permitted to run with fewer than 15 students and expressed concern that transfers could cause 
enrollment in those classes to fall further, potentially leading to courses being collapsed.  The 
administration was asked to continue monitoring that issue carefully so educational
August 10, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 14 of 36 
 
opportunities would not unintentionally be lost because of in-district transfers.  Superintendent 
Chmiel agreed. She explained that every approved transfer request had involved the building 
principal. Assistant superintendents contacted principals, reviewed transfer lists, examined 
school capacity, considered effects on schedules and individual courses, and then made 
decisions based on what was best for the school. She emphasized that transfers were not being 
approved by central administration without building-level input. 
8. Committee Member Stewart asked for clarification regarding the unusual number of transfer 
requests. Superintendent Chmiel explained that what was new was not necessarily schools 
reaching capacity, but the volume of 177 in-district requests to attend different schools under 
the new process.  Administration had established a protocol in which: 
 Transfer requests were received and acknowledged; 
 Requests were forwarded to the three assistant superintendents; 
 Requests were reviewed in groups or "buckets"; 
 Administration periodically determined what could and could not be approved; 
 Principals were consulted regarding the impact of each potential placement; and 
 Administration and principals maintained ongoing dialogue about enrollment, scheduling, 
and building capacity. 
Once the school year began and enrollment stabilized, the District planned to review how the 
process worked, what administration liked about it, what needed improvement, and what 
adjustments should be considered for the following fall. 
9. Committee Member Stewart then asked whether schools already at capacity were likely to 
remain at those levels.  Superintendent Chmiel explained that enrollment remained highly 
flexible during this time of year. Families may have moved during the summer without the 
District yet receiving notification, some families may have moved elsewhere within 
Manchester, and others may have left the City.  Once those movements were reflected in the 
enrollment data, administration would reassess capacity.  The Superintendent used Green Acres 
as an example, noting that the school had already been approaching capacity even before 
significant transfer activity.  She explained that enrollment decisions were affected by both:  
The amount and configuration of physical classroom space; and Available staffing. She stated 
that if classes appeared likely to exceed approximately 20 students at the elementary level or 25 
at the middle and high school levels, administration would explore ways to mitigate those
August 10, 2026, Board of School Committee

numbers, including the potential use of additional adults in the building.  She noted, however, 
that some schools historically reach capacity quickly because of physical limitations.

14. School Start Times 
 
Dr. Espinola provided an extensive update regarding the District's ongoing examination of school start 
times.  She stated that throughout the summer she had continued reviewing research regarding start 
times while also examining what a change would mean operationally for Manchester.  She had begun 
scheduling meetings with community partners to better understand the potential impact on: 
 Before- and after-school programming; 
 Child care; 
 Athletics; 
 Transportation; 
 Families; 
 Extracurricular activities; and 
 Staffing. 
 
Dr. Espinola stated that the more research she reviewed, the clearer the evidence became regarding 
adolescents.  She reported that the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends middle and high 
schools aim for start times no earlier than 8:30 a.m., based on adolescent sleep patterns and the 
relationship between adequate sleep and student health, safety, attendance, and academic success. 
She emphasized, however, that the issue could not be treated simply as a start-time conversation. 
Because Manchester operates a tiered transportation system, moving middle and high schools later 
would likely require elementary schools to begin earlier. 
 
Dr. Espinola reported that the research regarding earlier elementary start times was generally 
reassuring.  While earlier elementary schedules can result in somewhat less sleep and a slight increase 
in absenteeism, she stated that research generally found small or mixed effects on academic outcomes. 
When a school district using multiple bus runs must have one age group begin earlier, the research 
suggested elementary schools may be the more appropriate level in order to allow adolescent students 
to begin later. 
 
Dr. Espinola emphasized that research was only one component.  The District also needed to determine 
what a change would mean specifically for Manchester.  That required continued examination of child

and the overall impact on families.

throughout the District.  Its work would include:

 Working through operational details; 
 Gathering feedback; and
